---
title: "Learning Moment: Scope the Environment, Not the System"
date: 2026-10-14
categories: [claude, learning, ai-collaboration, linux, shell, python, teaching]
---

## Context

Installing a package from the AUR on Arch Linux with `yay`.
The package is an Electron app,
so its `PKGBUILD` downloads the upstream binary
and repacks it against the system `electron` runtime.
The repacking is done by `asar`,
installed from the Arch repositories as an ordinary system package.

The build never got that far.

## The Initial Ask

> i'm trying to install orca ade in arch linux. getting this error:

```
[user@host ~]$ yay -S orca-ide-bin
...
==> Starting prepare()...
Electron version: 43
file:///usr/lib/node_modules/@electron/asar/bin/asar.mjs:3
import packageJSON from '../package.json' with { type: 'json' };
                                          ^^^^

SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'with'
    at ModuleLoader.moduleStrategy (node:internal/modules/esm/translators:152:18)

Node.js v18.19.0
==> ERROR: A failure occurred in prepare().
    Aborting...
```

## Claude's Initial Response

The useful line is the one that looks like boilerplate: `Node.js v18.19.0`.

Arch is a rolling release.
Its `nodejs` package tracks the current release,
and there is no way a package freshly installed from the Arch repositories
is running on a Node from 2023.
So the question is not "why is `asar` broken"
but "why is this Node answering."

```bash
$ which -a node
~/.nvm/versions/node/v18.19.0/bin/node
/usr/bin/node

$ node --version
v18.19.0

$ /usr/bin/node --version
v26.11.1
```

Two Nodes, and the wrong one is first.
The rest follows:

```bash
$ ls -l /usr/bin/asar
/usr/bin/asar -> ../lib/node_modules/@electron/asar/bin/asar.mjs

$ head -3 /usr/lib/node_modules/@electron/asar/bin/asar.mjs
#!/usr/bin/env node

import packageJSON from '../package.json' with { type: 'json' };
```

`asar` is a system package, installed by `pacman`,
and its shebang is `#!/usr/bin/env node` — not `/usr/bin/node`.
It does not ask for *the system's* Node.
It asks for *whatever `node` means in this shell*,
and in this shell `node` means a version manager's copy of Node 18.19.0.

Import attributes (`with { type: 'json' }`) arrived in Node 18.20 and 20.10.
Run the exact same file under the Node that was actually installed alongside it,
and it is fine:

```bash
$ /usr/bin/node /usr/lib/node_modules/@electron/asar/bin/asar.mjs --version
v0.0.0-development
```

So Claude gave the fix — put the system Node first for the duration of the build:

```bash
PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH yay -S orca-ide-bin
```

and then added a second half, to stop it recurring:

```bash
nvm alias default system      # or: nvm alias default 24
```

## The Exchange

**Turn 1 — User:**

> can we use this skill to capture this learning moment […]
> it's about the importance of virtual environments
> and not changing system versions of things
> because it will affect other system tools.
> this is a similar concept in python
> and why we use venvs in python
> and other tools like uv, conda, pixi, pyenv, etc

**Turn 1 — Claude:**

The reframe lands on Claude's own second half.

`nvm alias default system` and `nvm alias default 24`
had been offered as interchangeable — pick whichever you like —
and they are not interchangeable at all.
They are the two sides of the lesson.

`nvm alias default system` says: *this machine's `node` is the system's `node`,
and my version manager speaks up only when a project asks it to.*

`nvm alias default 24` says: *this machine's `node` is Node 24, globally, for everything.*
Which is the exact sentence that caused the bug.
It was true of 18.19.0 too, on the day it was set,
when 18.19.0 was a perfectly reasonable thing to want.
Node 24 is simply the 18.19.0 of a few years from now.

The bug is not that the pinned version was old.
The bug is that a pin made for one project
became the answer to `node` for every process on the machine,
including a package build that has nothing to do with the project,
in a language ecosystem the user was not even thinking about at the time.

## The Final Solution

The one-off, for the build at hand — scoped to a single command,
changing nothing about the machine:

```bash
PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH yay -S orca-ide-bin
```

The standing fix — hand `node` back to the system,
and let the version manager be something a project opts into:

```bash
nvm alias default system
```

```bash
# in the project that actually needs Node 18
$ cd ~/projects/the-one-that-needs-18
$ echo "18.19.0" > .nvmrc
$ nvm use
Now using node v18.19.0
```

The version is now written down next to the code that requires it,
which is also the only place a reader would think to look for it.
Outside that directory, `node` is the system's Node,
and `asar` — a system package with a `#!/usr/bin/env node` shebang —
gets the Node it was installed next to.

The same shape, across ecosystems:

| Ecosystem | The trap | The scoped form |
|---|---|---|
| Node | `nvm alias default 18.19.0` | `.nvmrc` + `nvm use`, default left at `system` |
| Python | `pyenv global 3.11`, `pip install --user`, installing into the system interpreter | `python -m venv .venv`, `uv`, `pixi`, `conda` envs, `.python-version` per project |
| R | installing into the system library | `renv::init()` per project |
| Rust | `rustup default nightly` | `rust-toolchain.toml` in the repo |

Python is where most people meet this first,
and where the tooling is most insistent about it:
a virtual environment exists precisely so that
"this project needs `pandas` 1.5" is a fact about *the project*
and not a fact about *the computer*.
See also [A Program, or a Module?](2026-08-26-venv-is-a-module.qmd)
for what `venv` actually is when you go looking for it.

Everything above is the same idea with different file names.
And the failure mode is always the one that showed up here:
the damage does not appear in the project you configured.
It appears months later, in some unrelated tool,
which stops working for reasons that look like its own fault.

## The Lesson

**What Claude got right:**

The diagnosis, and the shape of the immediate fix.
Reading `Node.js v18.19.0` as the anomaly rather than the footer,
checking `which -a node` instead of the package,
and proving it by running the same file under `/usr/bin/node` —
that is the correct order of operations,
and it kept the user from filing a bug against a package that has none.

The immediate fix was correctly scoped, too.
`PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH yay -S …` changes one command's environment
and leaves no trace on the machine.
Claude reached for the narrow fix first without being asked to.

**What required human expertise:**

Recognising the bug as an instance of a class.

To Claude this was a Node version problem on an Arch box.
To someone who teaches environments for a living
it is the canonical example of why environments are scoped:
a global default is a claim about every process on the machine,
made by someone who was thinking about one project.

That recognition is what exposed the flaw in the advice.
Claude offered `nvm alias default system` and `nvm alias default 24`
as a matter of taste.
Someone holding the general principle can see immediately
that one of them is the lesson and the other is the bug with a fresher number on it.

**Why Claude missed it:**

*The stated goal was the whole frame.*
"Make this install work" was the ask, and both halves of the answer do that.
The second half also quietly re-arms the trap,
but only for a build that has not happened yet,
asked about by a user who has not asked yet.
Nothing in the question pointed at the future.

*A stale value, not a stale mechanism.*
Claude read `18.19.0` as the wrong **number** and reached for a better number.
The number was never the problem.
The problem is a pin that outlives the reason it was set,
and swapping in Node 24 preserves that property perfectly.
Fixing the value where the mechanism is at fault is a very easy mistake to make
when the value is sitting right there in the error message, looking wrong.

*No view of elapsed time.*
18.19.0 was presumably pinned on purpose, for something, on a day when it was correct.
Claude sees the end state and none of the months in between —
the months in which a deliberate, local, reasonable choice
quietly became the global answer to `node`
for a package manager building software in a different ecosystem entirely.
The cost of a global pin is paid later, by a different tool, in a different context.
That is exactly the kind of cost a single-session view cannot see.

*The symptom and the cause were in different ecosystems.*
The error was a Node syntax error inside a Node tool,
so the investigation stayed in Node-land and produced a Node-land answer.
But the cause is a PATH-ordering policy that spans every language on the machine.
The evidence was literally on screen:

```
PATH=/usr/share/positron/bin:~/.nvm/versions/node/v18.19.0/bin:
     ~/.pyenv/shims:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:...
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
             same position, same mechanism, different language
```

Claude printed that line while diagnosing, used the `nvm` entry, and read right past the rest.
Having answered the Node question, it stopped looking —
even though the generalisation was sitting three colons to the right.

**Worth noting — the machine was already half-right.**

On the Python side of the same box, the principle was already in force:

```bash
$ pyenv version
system (set by ~/.python-version)
```

The global pyenv version is `system`.
The shims are ahead of `/usr/bin` in `PATH`, exactly like nvm's,
but they resolve to the system interpreter and get out of the way,
so a system tool with `#!/usr/bin/env python3` gets the Python it was installed next to.

So this was not someone learning the idea for the first time.
It was someone who had already applied it,
in the ecosystem that teaches it loudest,
and had one version manager in another ecosystem
left quietly pinned to a number set for a project long since finished.

Which is the most honest version of the lesson:
knowing the principle is not the same as having it configured everywhere,
and the place you have not configured it
will tell you about it in the least convenient way it can.

**Key takeaway:**

A version manager's global default is a decision about every tool on the machine,
not just about your project —
so pin the version next to the project that needs it,
and leave the system pointing at the system.
